title: Generative AI as a Learning Buddy and a Teaching Assistant: Preservice Teachers’ Use and Attitudes
extended_summary:
This paper examines how preservice teachers use generative AI in teacher education, with a particular focus on the Global South context of Ghana. The study asks what specific academic and instructional tasks preservice teachers use GenAI for, how frequently they use it, what attitudes they hold toward it, and whether demographic factors such as age, gender, and class level predict usage or attitudes. The motivation is that although GenAI is rapidly entering education, there is limited evidence on how preservice teachers in under-resourced contexts are actually engaging with these tools.

The study uses a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 167 preservice teachers from four teacher education institutions in Ghana. Participants completed a structured questionnaire covering demographics, frequency of GenAI use, specific use cases, and attitudes toward GenAI. The paper frames GenAI in two roles: as a “learning buddy” for personal academic support and as a “teaching assistant” for instructional planning. Analyses included descriptive statistics, multiple regression, and ordinal logistic regression.

The participants were undergraduate preservice teachers enrolled in Bachelor of Education programs, mainly in Levels 300 and 400, in Ghanaian teacher education institutions. In this context, students are simultaneously engaged in coursework and supported school-based teaching practice, while also facing infrastructural barriers such as costly internet data and limited connectivity. The data were collected online through Google Forms over a maximum period of four weeks.

The main findings are that preservice teachers used GenAI most often as a learning buddy for finding reading materials, obtaining in-depth explanations, and locating practical examples. As a teaching assistant, they most often used it to find teaching resources, identify assessment strategies, and develop lesson-related materials. Overall use was more frequent for academic learning than for instructional preparation. Attitudes toward GenAI were generally positive, with participants reporting that it supported autonomy in learning and teaching preparation, though concerns remained about cost, output inaccuracy, and academic dishonesty. Demographic variables did not significantly predict attitudes, but class level and age predicted some usage patterns, with more advanced students generally reporting greater use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools/chatbots used for learning support and teaching preparation, with no single specific product evaluated as the focal intervention.
identified_tools.use_case: Preservice teachers in Ghana reported using GenAI as a 'learning buddy' for finding reading materials, obtaining in-depth explanations, practical examples, and reflections, and as a 'teaching assistant' for finding teaching resources, assessment strategies, lesson objectives, lesson plans, and sample lessons.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of preservice teachers, GenAI was used more frequently for academic learning than for instructional preparation. For learning-buddy use, 28.14% reported using GenAI 'Very Often,' 16.17% 'Often,' and 43.11% 'Sometimes'; for teaching-assistant use, 14.97% reported 'Very Often,' 18.56% 'Often,' and 36.53% 'Sometimes.'
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of GenAI use for academic learning and instructional preparation

findings.finding_summary: Preservice teachers reported positive attitudes toward GenAI for learning and teaching tasks. The highest-rated learning items were 'With the help of GenAI, I am able to get more reading materials' (M=4.02, SD=0.93) and 'GenAI helped me understand various complex areas of my study' (M=3.98, SD=0.85); for teaching, 'GenAI has the potential to improve my pedagogical skills' received M=3.88, SD=0.90, and support for incorporating GenAI into courses/practicum was M=3.78, SD=1.00.
findings.measure: Item-level attitudes on GenAI for Learning and GenAI for Teaching scales

findings.finding_summary: Participants also reported concerns about GenAI cost, trust, and academic dishonesty. 'It is expensive to use GenAI tools for teaching' was rated M=3.17, SD=1.13; 'The information provided by GenAI tools was not accurate enough, so I never trusted them' was rated M=2.62, SD=1.07; and concern that 'Most students might cheat and will not develop critical and creative skills due to GenAI' was M=3.28, SD=1.31.
findings.measure: Item-level ethical, accuracy, and barrier perceptions

findings.finding_summary: Demographic factors did not significantly predict attitudes toward GenAI overall, but some demographics predicted usage frequency. Multiple regression showed attitudes were not predicted by age, gender, and class level, F(3,163)=.319, p=.811, R2=.006. Ordinal logistic regression for learning use was significant, likelihood ratio χ2(6)=16.651, p=.011, with Age 16-20 years (B=-2.880, SE=1.280, p=.024) and Class Level 300 (B=.886, SE=.342, p=.010) as significant predictors; for teaching use, the model was also significant, χ2(6)=16.905, p=.01, with Class Level 200 (B=-1.693, SE=.666, p=.011) significant.
findings.measure: Regression-predicted attitudes and self-reported usage frequency by demographic variables

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical cross-sectional survey using descriptive statistics and regression analyses, but it is observational and based on self-report rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceptions and usage patterns, but no causal learning effects or standardized effect sizes on student outcomes are provided, so impact remains unclear.
